common_name: Director George T. Moore Water Lily (Classic Fragrant Tropical Violet-Purple Day-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Director George T. Moore, a classic 1941 Missouri Botanical Garden introduction, bears fragrant, star-shaped, violet-purple day-blooming flowers.

directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F, since tropical water lilies are cold-sensitive and grow poorly if planted too early. Director George T. Moore, introduced in 1941 by the Missouri Botanical Garden and named for its longtime director, is a classic, long-cultivated tropical water lily bearing large, star-shaped flowers in a rich violet-purple with a sweet, distinctive fragrance, opening during the day above the water's surface on strong stems held well above the pads. It is a vigorous grower, producing abundant bloom through the warm season, and in zones below its perennial range is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and divide congested tubers as needed.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Perry's Baby Red Water Lily (Dwarf Hardy Deep Red Container Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 6-12 inches deep in a full-sun pond or tub after last frost; Perry's Baby Red, a 1989 introduction, is a true dwarf hardy water lily bearing deep red cup-shaped flowers, ideal for small ponds and container water gardens.

directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers only 6 to 12 inches deep in a full-sun pond or even a half-barrel tub garden, since Perry's Baby Red is a genuine dwarf, staying small enough that it does not need the large ponds most hardy water lilies require. Introduced in 1989 by hybridizer D. Stetson Perry, it bears compact, cup-shaped flowers in a deep, rich red held just above small, neat pads, making it one of the best hardy water lily choices for a container water garden, small preformed pond, or any spot too small for a standard cultivar. It overwinters in the pond in most temperate climates as a true hardy type. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and divide congested rhizomes every few years.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Wood's White Knight Water Lily (Huge Fragrant Night-Blooming Tropical White)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Wood's White Knight bears huge, fragrant, night-blooming white flowers 10-12 inches across with 28-30 petals.

directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F. Wood's White Knight is one of the largest-flowered night-blooming tropical water lilies in cultivation, producing enormous, richly fragrant white blooms 10 to 12 inches across with 28 to 30 slender petals, opening in the evening and remaining open into the following morning, making it a spectacular choice for a pond viewed at dusk or enjoyed with evening entertaining. It is a vigorous grower requiring a fairly large pond to accommodate its substantial pads and flowers. In zones below its perennial range it is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season and remove spent flowers and yellowing pads.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Panama Pacific Water Lily (Historic Viviparous Violet-Purple Tropical Day-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Panama Pacific, introduced in 1914, is a viviparous tropical day-bloomer producing small plantlets directly on the leaf surface, and shows somewhat better cold tolerance than most tropical water lilies.

directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F. Panama Pacific, introduced in 1914 and still grown over a century later, bears rich violet-purple, star-shaped day-blooming flowers, and is notable among tropical water lilies for being viviparous, sprouting small new plantlets directly on the leaf surface that can be detached and grown into new plants, an easy and reliable propagation method. It also shows somewhat better cold tolerance than many other tropical cultivars, extending its useful range a bit further into cooler zones before winter dormancy sets in. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and detach and pot up plantlets as they form.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Pink Pickerelweed (Pink-Flowered Native Marginal Pond Plant)

planting.note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; Pink Pons is a pink-flowered sport of the usually blue-flowered native pickerelweed.

directions: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun. Pink Pons is a naturally occurring pink-flowered sport of native pickerelweed, an easy-to-grow, tough marginal aquatic normally seen with blue-violet flower spikes, offering an unusual soft pink color option on the same reliable, glossy heart-shaped foliage and upright habit. It blooms over a long season from late spring into fall, drawing bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds to its flower spikes, and provides habitat and cover for pond wildlife. As a true native wetland plant, it tolerates a wide range of water depths and spreads gradually by rhizomes to form an increasing colony at the pond edge. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and control spread.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Double Japanese Arrowhead (Old World Fully Double White-Flowered Arrowhead)

planting.note: Plant tubers or divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; this Old World arrowhead species bears fully double white flowers, distinct from the single-flowered native arrowhead species.

directions: Plant tubers or divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun. This Old World arrowhead, native across Europe and Asia, is grown in cultivation almost exclusively in its fully double form, bearing showy, pompom-like white flowers with many extra petal segments in place of the simple three-petaled bloom of the wild species, a distinctly more ornamental flower than the native North American Sagittaria species more commonly planted. Its arrow-shaped leaves rise above the water on sturdy stems, providing vertical accent and cover for pond wildlife at the margin. It spreads by tubers to form a colony over time; divide and thin every few years to control spread and maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Double Yellow Flag Iris (Slower-Spreading Double-Flowered Yellow Flag)

planting.note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers or at the pond margin in full sun to partial shade in spring; this double-flowered yellow flag iris grows notably less vigorously and spreads more slowly than the straight species, which is considered invasive in some regions.

directions: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers or directly at the pond margin in full sun to partial shade, and check local regulations before planting, since the straight species of yellow flag iris is classed as invasive in parts of North America. This double-flowered selection bears extra petal segments crowded into a fuller, showier bloom than the simple three-petaled species flower, in the same bright golden yellow, and, notably, grows and spreads considerably less vigorously than the aggressive wild form, making it a more garden-appropriate choice where the species itself would be discouraged. It tolerates standing water as well as consistently moist soil at the pond edge, forming an upright clump of sword-like foliage. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Giant Flatsedge (Mexican Papyrus, New World Coastal Umbrella Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Giant Flatsedge, native from the Gulf Coast through the Caribbean and Latin America, is a New World relative of Egyptian papyrus, taller with smaller flower umbels.

directions: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, or directly in a boggy, permanently wet spot. Giant Flatsedge, native from the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana through the Caribbean and much of Latin America, is the New World counterpart to Egyptian papyrus, producing tall, thick, triangular stems topped with a burst of thin, drooping bracts, though its individual flower umbels are smaller and more delicate than true Egyptian papyrus. Its imposing height and bold, architectural silhouette make it an excellent vertical accent and privacy screen at a Gulf Coast pond edge, and as a regional native it tolerates the area's heat, humidity, and seasonal flooding without complaint. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and control spread.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Erebus Longwood Water Canna (True Aquatic Coral-Pink Submerged-Culture Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; Erebus, bred at Longwood Gardens specifically for true aquatic, submerged culture, bears coral-pink flowers over blue-green striped foliage.

directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, once all frost danger has passed. Erebus is one of a small group of true aquatic water cannas bred at Longwood Gardens specifically to thrive with their crowns and lower stems submerged, unlike ordinary garden canna, which will rot if kept constantly wet at the root. It bears clear coral-pink flowers above handsome, blue-green foliage marked with subtle striping, adding bold tropical texture and color to the pond margin through the warm season. In zones below its perennial range, lift and store the rhizome indoors over winter like standard canna. Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Ra Longwood Water Canna (Tall Soft-Yellow True Aquatic Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; Ra, a companion to the Longwood aquatic canna breeding line, is the tallest of the trio, bearing soft yellow flowers.

directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, once all frost danger has passed. Ra is a true aquatic water canna bred at Longwood Gardens for submerged culture, the tallest of the Longwood aquatic canna introductions, reaching well over the height of ordinary garden canna and forming a dramatic vertical accent at the back of the pond margin, topped with soft, clear yellow flowers through the warm season. Unlike ordinary garden canna, it thrives with its crown and lower stems kept constantly submerged rather than rotting in wet soil. In zones below its perennial range, lift and store the rhizome indoors over winter like standard canna. Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Perry's Giant Sunburst Lotus (Large Lemon-Yellow Slocum Hybrid Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed past last frost; Perry's Giant Sunburst, bred by Perry D. Slocum, bears large lemon-yellow flowers 8-12 inches across.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed past danger of frost. Perry's Giant Sunburst, bred by the renowned lotus and water lily hybridizer Perry D. Slocum, bears enormous, richly fragrant lemon-yellow flowers 8 to 12 inches across held well above the water on tall, sturdy stems, one of the largest-flowered yellow lotus cultivars available, followed by the distinctive flat seed pods prized for dried arrangements. Once the huge, round, umbrella-like leaves and blooms emerge in early summer, the plant grows vigorously and needs a fairly large, deep container or open pond bottom to reach its full size. Lotus goes dormant and dies back completely each winter, re-emerging from the tuber the following late spring; divide overcrowded tubers every few years in spring.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Black Truffle Cardinal Flower (Near-Black Spring Foliage Scarlet Lobelia)

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Black Truffle emerges with near-black spring foliage that ages to maroon, bearing the classic scarlet cardinal flower blooms.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or any low spot that stays reliably damp. Black Truffle is a patented cardinal flower selection prized for its striking near-black spring foliage, which gradually ages to a rich deep maroon through summer, providing months of dramatic foliage color in addition to the tall, brilliant scarlet flower spikes that draw hummingbirds heavily from mid to late summer. Its dark leaves make an especially strong contrast against the vivid red blooms, more dramatic than the plain green foliage of the straight species. Cardinal flower is naturally short-lived but self-sows and can be divided to maintain a planting; keep soil consistently moist, since it does not tolerate drought.

common_name: Ajax Rain Lily (Classic Straw-Yellow-Fading-White Hybrid Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ajax, a classic hybrid of Zephyranthes candida and Z. citrina, bears straw-yellow flowers that fade to white, flushing into bloom after summer rains.

directions: Plant bulbs 1 to 2 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ajax is a classic, long-cultivated hybrid rain lily, a cross of Zephyranthes candida and Z. citrina, bearing crocus-like flowers that open a warm straw-yellow and gradually fade toward white as they age, giving a two-toned effect across a single flush of bloom. Like other rain lilies, it flowers in sudden, reliable flushes triggered by a good soaking rain after a dry spell, particularly through the warm months, making a naturalized planting appear to bloom almost overnight. It is hardy and drought-tolerant once established, multiplying gradually by bulb offsets to form an increasing clump or drift at the border edge, along a walkway, or naturalized in a lawn area that isn't mowed too closely. Essentially carefree once planted, needing no regular care beyond occasional division of crowded clumps.

common_name: Carolina Fanwort (Feathery Native Submerged Oxygenating Pond Plant)

planting.note: Plant weighted bunches or rooted stems directly in the pond, fully submerged, in full sun to partial shade after last frost; Carolina Fanwort is a classic feathery, fine-textured submerged oxygenator native to the southeastern US, helping keep pond water clear.

directions: Plant weighted bunches of cuttings or rooted stems directly in the pond substrate or a submerged planting basket, fully underwater, in full sun to partial shade. Carolina Fanwort is a native submerged aquatic with finely divided, feathery, fan-shaped underwater foliage in soft green to reddish-bronze tones, growing entirely below the surface aside from small floating leaves and tiny white to pale purple flowers that occasionally reach the surface in summer. As a submerged oxygenator, it helps maintain healthy pond water quality by absorbing excess nutrients that would otherwise fuel algae growth and by releasing oxygen into the water, benefiting fish and other pond life, while its dense underwater growth provides cover for fry and other small aquatic creatures. It grows vigorously in nutrient-rich water and may need periodic thinning to prevent it from overtaking a smaller pond.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

planting.note: Float or lightly root plants in the pond, fully or partially submerged, in partial shade to full sun after all frost danger has passed; Water Sprite is an unusual floating or submerged fern, entirely distinct in form and habit from any terrestrial garden fern.

directions: Float plants freely on the pond surface or lightly anchor rooted stock in a submerged planting basket, in partial shade to full sun, in warm, calm water. Water Sprite is an unusual true fern that grows either floating on the water's surface or fully submerged, with finely divided, lacy, bright green fronds that provide fine-textured contrast to broader-leaved pond plants, entirely different in form and habit from any terrestrial fern grown in the garden. It reproduces readily by tiny plantlets that form along the frond margins, dropping off to grow into new plants and quickly multiplying to cover open water, which also makes it valuable as shelter and spawning habitat for pond fish and as a nutrient-absorbing plant that helps keep water clear. It is frost-tender and treated as a warm-season plant outside the mildest zones, either replaced annually or overwintered indoors in an aquarium or heated container.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Water Snowflake (White Fringed-Petal Floating Pond Plant)

planting.note: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after all frost danger has passed; Water Snowflake bears small, white, fringed-petal flowers above floating heart-shaped pads, distinct from the yellow-flowered Nymphoides already common in cultivation.

directions: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 4 to 12 inches deep in a full-sun pond. Water Snowflake produces small, rounded, heart-shaped floating pads resembling miniature water lily leaves, with delicate white flowers whose petal edges are finely fringed and frilled, giving each bloom a lacy, snowflake-like texture, opening in succession through the warm months just above the water's surface. It spreads by runners to cover open water, providing shade that helps suppress algae while remaining light and airy in appearance compared to bolder-leaved pond plants. It is frost-tender and best suited to warm, frost-free ponds; in cooler zones it can be grown as a summer annual or overwintered indoors. Thin and divide regularly, since it spreads readily in favorable conditions.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Variegated Water Clover (Mottled Bicolor Four-Leaf Floating Fern Ally)

planting.note: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in shallow submerged containers in a full-sun to partial-shade pond after all frost danger has passed; Variegated Water Clover bears distinctive mottled bicolor four-part leaves floating on the water's surface.

directions: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in shallow submerged containers just a few inches deep, in full sun to partial shade. Variegated Water Clover produces distinctive four-part leaves that closely resemble a four-leaf clover, floating flat on the water's surface, each leaflet attractively mottled in bands of green and yellow-green, a more striking, patterned foliage effect than the plain green Marsilea species more commonly grown. This unusual fern relative spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a low, textural mat over shallow water or damp mud, useful at a pond margin, in a bog garden, or in a shallow water feature. It is frost-tender and best suited to warm, frost-free ponds year-round; in cooler zones grow as a summer annual or overwinter indoors. Thin spreading colonies periodically to keep them in bounds.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Watermeal (World's Smallest Flowering Plant, Native Floating Novelty)

planting.note: Scatter a starter colony directly onto calm pond water in full sun to partial shade after last frost; Watermeal is a native, rootless, free-floating relative of duckweed and is considered the world's smallest flowering plant, valued as a novelty and as fish and waterfowl forage.

directions: Scatter a small starter colony directly onto calm, still pond water in full sun to partial shade, where it will multiply rapidly on its own. Watermeal consists of tiny, rootless, oval green grains barely visible to the naked eye, individually among the smallest flowering plants known to science, floating in dense colonies that can carpet the water's surface in favorable, nutrient-rich conditions. Though easy to dismiss as a nuisance, it is a valuable natural food source for fish, ducks, and other waterfowl, and, like duckweed, absorbs excess nutrients from the water that would otherwise feed algae blooms. It multiplies extremely quickly in warm, nutrient-rich water and can cover a pond's surface faster than duckweed, so thin regularly with a net or skimmer if full coverage isn't wanted, since a thick surface mat can block light and oxygen exchange for submerged plants and fish below.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society
